caption: County of Los Angeles v. Mendez
node: use-of-force-and-liability/Use of Force (also Section 1983 Liability and Qualified Immunity)
justification: Unanimous. REJECTED the Ninth Circuit's 'provocation rule' — an officer's otherwise-reasonable use of force is NOT rendered unreasonable merely because the officer committed a separate Fourth Amendment violation (unlawful warrantless entry) that provoked the confrontation. Excessive-force reasonableness is analyzed under Graham on its own terms; a distinct antecedent 4A violation is redressed on its own (proximate-cause) footing, not by bootstrapping. Controlling SCOTUS use-of-force/§1983 decision the corpus entirely LACKS (grep: 'provocation' 0; 'County of Los Angeles' 0). Directly frames the officer-created-danger question Barnes v. Felix (in corpus) expressly left open. Strong page-candidate.
gate: INGEST prong (a) field conduct + (c) officer civil-liability exposure
notes: Not in GAP; distinct from US v. Mendez (7th Cir. border) and US v. August. Anchors the officer-created-danger split row below.

caption: Manuel v. City of Joliet
node: use-of-force-and-liability/Malicious Prosecution under the Fourth Amendment
justification: 6-2 (Kagan, J.). The Fourth Amendment governs a claim for unlawful PRETRIAL DETENTION even AFTER the start of legal process — detention pursuant to legal process that is itself unsupported by probable cause (here 48 days on a fabricated field-test) is an unreasonable seizure actionable under §1983. The controlling SCOTUS predicate for the Fourth-Amendment malicious-prosecution / unlawful-detention theory. Corpus LACKS it (grep: 'Manuel v. City of Joliet' 0; the lone 'Manuel' hit is a first name in Flores-Montano). Distinct from GAP's Thompson v. Clark (favorable-termination element) and Chiaverini (charge-specific PC) — Manuel establishes the claim exists; not in GAP. Anchors the Malicious Prosecution stub node.
gate: INGEST prong (b) admissibility/seizure + (c) officer civil-liability exposure
notes: Not in GAP. Predecessor to Thompson v. Clark (2022, GAP) — fold-relationship for S6/R9 to note, but Manuel's own holding (claim exists) is load-bearing => own page.

caption: Timbs v. Indiana
justification: Unanimous (Ginsburg, J.). The Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause is incorporated against the States via the Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause, and it applies to civil in rem forfeitures that are at least partly punitive (seizure of a $42k Land Rover for a drug offense). The keystone modern constraint on state/local civil asset forfeiture and the anchor of the Civil Asset Forfeiture placed-empty node (a STUB with ZERO cases; grep 'Timbs' 0). Controlling SCOTUS, expressly in remit per R2(c)+D6 (forfeiture boundary markers).
gate: INGEST prong (c) officer civil-liability / forfeiture boundary (R2(c), D6)
notes: Not in GAP (GAP's forfeiture case is Culley 2024 on hearing-timing). Timbs = the incorporation/excessive-fines anchor.

caption: Austin v. United States
justification: The Excessive Fines Clause applies to civil in rem forfeiture proceedings because such forfeitures serve at least in part to punish ('as punishment for some offense'). The doctrinal predicate Timbs incorporates against the States. Controlling SCOTUS; corpus lacks it (grep 'Austin v. United States' 0). Forfeiture node anchor.
notes: Not in GAP. Pairs with Timbs + Bajakajian on the Civil Asset Forfeiture page.

caption: United States v. Bajakajian
justification: Sets the excessive-fines TEST — a forfeiture is unconstitutional if 'grossly disproportional to the gravity of the defendant's offense' (a $357,144 currency forfeiture for a failure-to-report violation was grossly disproportionate). The operative proportionality standard applied under Timbs/Austin. Controlling SCOTUS; corpus lacks it (grep 'Bajakajian' 0). Forfeiture node anchor.
notes: Not in GAP. Completes the excessive-fines trio (Austin -> Timbs -> Bajakajian test).

caption: United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property
justification: Absent exigent circumstances, the Due Process Clause requires NOTICE and a hearing BEFORE the Government may seize REAL PROPERTY for civil forfeiture; the Fourth Amendment does not independently answer the timing question, but due process constrains it. Directly bears on officer/agency FIELD CONDUCT (when property may be seized). Controlling SCOTUS; corpus lacks it (grep 'James Daniel Good' 0). Forfeiture node anchor for the seizure-timing/procedural-due-process line.
gate: INGEST prong (a) field conduct (seizure) + (c) forfeiture boundary
notes: Not in GAP. Pairs with Culley (2024, GAP, timely-hearing) as the procedural-due-process anchor; distinct question (pre-seizure notice for real property).

caption: Bennis v. Michigan
justification: An 'innocent owner' defense is NOT constitutionally required in civil in rem forfeiture — a co-owner's car could be forfeited despite her lack of knowledge of the criminal use (public-nuisance abatement). Controlling SCOTUS on the outer limit of forfeiture's reach against innocent owners; corpus lacks it (grep 'Bennis' 0). Forfeiture node — the innocent-owner boundary. (Borderline vs mention given age/frequency; recommend page under D1 flip since the node is a stub and this is the controlling innocent-owner authority.)
notes: Not in GAP. If S6 opts to trim the forfeiture set, Bennis/Calero-Toledo are the two most droppable-to-mention; Timbs/Austin/Bajakajian/Good are the core.

caption: Calero-Toledo v. Pearson Yacht Leasing Co.
justification: Foundational modern in rem forfeiture case — upheld forfeiture of a leased yacht used (without the lessor's knowledge) to carry marijuana, and articulated the historical 'innocent owner' / property-guilt fiction and the (limited) due-process pre-seizure exception for movable property. The doctrinal ancestor of Bennis/Good/Austin. Controlling SCOTUS; corpus lacks it (grep 'Calero-Toledo' 0). (Borderline page vs mention — older foundational; recommend page as the historical anchor of the forfeiture node, or fold as history per PRACTICES §7.)
notes: Not in GAP. Candidate for history-rendering (PRACTICES §7) given its age and the innocent-owner fiction later constrained by Timbs.

caption: Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach
justification: Narrow retaliatory-arrest holding: the existence of probable cause does NOT categorically bar a §1983 First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim where the plaintiff alleges an official MUNICIPAL POLICY of retaliation (as opposed to a split-second individual arrest). The SCOTUS predecessor that framed the probable-cause bar question later answered generally in Nieves (2019, GAP) and refined in Gonzalez v. Trevino (2024, GAP). Corpus lacks it (grep 'Lozman' 0). Retaliatory Arrest stub anchor.
gate: INGEST prong (c) officer civil-liability exposure (First Amendment retaliatory arrest)
notes: Not in GAP (GAP = Nieves + Gonzalez). Adjacent cluster; Lozman's own municipal-policy carve-out is distinct/load-bearing => own page (or fold into the Retaliatory Arrest node with Nieves/Gonzalez per S6 discretion).

caption: Hernandez v. Mesa
node: use-of-force-and-liability/Section 1983 Liability and Qualified Immunity (Bivens boundary)
justification: Bivens does NOT extend to a cross-border shooting (a Border Patrol agent's cross-border shooting of a Mexican national) — a new context implicating foreign relations/national security; a paradigmatic post-Abbasi refusal to imply a Bivens remedy. Controlling SCOTUS Bivens-boundary marker within R2(c). Corpus LACKS it (grep 'Hernandez v. Mesa' 0) though it treats sibling Bivens-limit cases Abbasi and Egbert as page-less mentions. BORDERLINE: recommend page under D1 flip (SCOTUS, gate-passing), but S6 may fold as a mention consistent with its Abbasi/Egbert treatment.
notes: Not in GAP. Flag for the borderline packet (packet B) if S6 keeps Bivens-limit cases page-less — disposition should match Abbasi/Egbert for consistency (Egbert is a GAP AUTHOR under D6, which argues FOR paging Hernandez too).

caption: Officer-created-danger / pre-seizure-reckless-conduct circuit split
justification: SPLIT-MARKER (both sides, circuits named). Barnes v. Felix (2025, in corpus) resolved the TEMPORAL question (totality has no time limit; 'moment-of-threat' rejected) but expressly LEFT OPEN whether an officer's own reckless/unconstitutional PRE-SEIZURE conduct that created the need for force bears on 4A reasonableness. Post-Mendez (2017), circuits divide: BROAD view — pre-seizure reckless conduct is part of the totality (1st, 7th, 9th, 10th Cir.; e.g., 10th Cir. Allen v. Muskogee, 119 F.3d 837 (1997); 9th Cir. Billington v. Smith, 292 F.3d 1177 (2002)); NARROW view — it is not (2d, 4th Cir.). County of Los Angeles v. Mendez (above) is the SCOTUS anchor that cabins the theory (a separate 4A violation does not auto-render force unreasonable). Meets the D5 floor as a both-sides/circuits-named split-marker.
notes: S2 to confirm the current representative captions per side (post-Barnes reframing may have re-decided some). Recommend: page County of L.A. v. Mendez as the anchor + carry the circuit split as a Recent-developments split block on Use of Force with both sides named; individual circuit cases enter as lower-court-development bullets unless S7 prose relies on one.
